name: PT Impack Pratama Industri Tbk
industry_name: Industrial goods, building products & electrical equipment

frontmatter.title: Impack Pratama: a real franchise priced for growth it has never sustained
frontmatter.summary: Hold SELL, target Rp277 against Rp775, a -63.5% total return. A genuine premium franchise on 49.8x forward earnings and 10.7x book, but the reverse DCF needs 32.9% revenue growth in FY2027E sustained for a decade, where the company plans IDR5,100.0bn of FY2026 revenue and grew 12.0% per cent in the third quarter. Revision: DCF now carries the great majority of the target.
thesis: The franchise earns its keep: FY2025 revenue of 4,271.5 at a 39.5% gross margin and a 22.4% return on equity, with operating cash flow covering profit and capex [S7, S4]. Nine-month 2026 revenue of 3,723 IDR bn and net profit of 640 IDR bn already beat the whole of FY2025 on profit [S8].

The price is a different claim. At Rp775 the shares trade on 49.8x our FY2026E earnings, 10.7x book and a 1.6% free-cash-flow-to-equity yield [S0]; the reverse DCF needs 32.9% revenue growth in FY2027E sustained at high-twenties through FY2035E, against a company plan of IDR5,100.0bn for FY2026 that it has kept unchanged [S10].

Cash conversion is honest, but the business is capital-hungry: trade working capital was IDR1,683.6bn at end-2025, about two-fifths of revenue, so every extra rupiah of growth needs funding, and free cash flow to the firm of 606.4 is a thin yield on the equity value [S7, S8].

DCF is the primary method and now carries the great majority of the target. The peer set is Indonesian cement, ceramics, cable and sanitary ware on 7.6 times earnings, which this report calls a floor for a premium franchise, so a floor cannot be two-fifths of fair value [S0].

Capital allocation is the governance story: the company issued new equity in 2025 and then bought 222 m sharesm shares back in 2026 at more than twice the current price, while a related-party acquisition left IDR677.0bn in a common-control debit. Neither a family sell-down nor a rising free float is supported by the filings [S8, S7, S9].

blocks.text: We hold our **SELL** rating on PT Impack Pratama Industri with a twelve-month target of **Rp277**, a -63.5% return from the Rp775 price including the Rp5 dividend we expect over the year [S0].

This revision moves the target from the draft and corrects three errors in it. The target is higher because the DCF now carries the great majority of the blend rather than the draft two-fifths: a peer median this report calls a floor cannot be two-fifths of fair value. Margins are held at the last actual instead of faded without a source, the recurring other income the company reports in consecutive periods is carried inside operating profit rather than dropped, and trade working capital is rebuilt from the LK rather than from the vendor's netted measure. Separately, the draft's claim that the controlling family sold down through 2026 is wrong and is withdrawn: the family blocks are unchanged at 30 September 2026 and the free-float figure fell because of the company's own buyback [S8, S9].

The company is not the problem. Impack makes premium plastic and composite building materials under brands that contractors and renovators ask for by name, sells them through a distribution network built over decades, and manufactures in five countries [S9]. It earned 4,271.5 of revenue in FY2025 at a 39.5% gross margin and a 22.4% return on equity, converted most of its profit into cash, and was audited without qualification [S7, S9]. Nine-month 2026 revenue of 3,723 IDR bn and net profit attributable to shareholders of 640 IDR bn show the business accelerating, not fading [S8].

The problem is the price. At Rp775 the shares are on 49.8x our FY2026E earnings, 10.7x book value and 30.8x EBITDA [S0]. For that to be fair, growth has to be both faster and longer than the company has ever delivered: our reverse DCF solves to 32.9% revenue growth in FY2027E, and because the solver applies that increment to every forecast year the requirement is a sustained path of high-twenties growth to FY2030E, not a one-year jump. The variant view is not that Impack is a bad business. It is that the market is paying a compounder's terminal multiple for a company whose own plan, IDR5,100.0bn of FY2026 revenue, we take at face value [S10].

Three things move the value. First, the revenue path: we grow revenue from 4,271.5 in FY2025 to 7,951.0 in FY2030E and fade to terminal growth after that; the price embeds growth well above 10.0% for far longer. Second, the gross margin: 40.0% in FY2026E is the nine-month actual held flat, and a two-point miss costs roughly a fifth of the DCF value. Third, capital intensity: trade working capital absorbs 36.0% of revenue, so every extra rupiah of growth needs funding, and the value falls when that ratio rises [S7, S8].
The quality is worth owning at a price. It is not worth owning at this one.

Impack Pratama Industri is an Indonesian building-materials group founded in 1981 and listed on the main board of the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2024 [S9]. It manufactures and distributes plastic sheet roofing, polycarbonate and uPVC roofing, fibre-reinforced polyester sheeting, PVC pipe, ceiling and cladding products, adhesives and interior products, and it owns Altira Business Park in North Jakarta through a property subsidiary [S9]. The range is deliberately wide: the group competes in premium roofing, cladding and interior finishes rather than in commodity cement or steel, and it sells under brands such as Alderon, Solartuff, Decobond and Impraboard that carry a price premium in the trade [S9].

The group reports three segments. Manufacturing produced 3,077 IDR bn of segment revenue before eliminations in FY2025 and 966 IDR bn of segment profit before tax; distribution produced 3,719 IDR bn of segment revenue, mostly sales of the group's own manufactured products through the trade, and a thin profit; real estate is small and dominated by Altira [S7]. Inter-segment sales are eliminated, so segment revenues sum to well above the consolidated 4,271.5. The economic read is simple: manufacturing earns the margin, distribution earns the reach, and property is a small land bank.

Manufacturing runs across plants in five countries [S6, S9]. In Indonesia the plants are at Cikarang and Karawang in West Java, Bekasi and Batang in Central Java; abroad the group manufactures in Vietnam, Singapore and Australia, including an FRP roofing plant in Melbourne [S9]. The Batang factory began operating in 2024 and the Cikarang distribution centre was completed in the same year; in 2025 the company added uPVC roofing lines at Cikarang and Batang, expanded FRP capacity in Melbourne and launched a recycled-roofing line that turns multilayer plastic waste into building sheet [S9]. That is a sensible use of a manufacturing base: add capacity where demand is, and add a product that turns a waste cost into a margin.

The strategy is regional, not only national. Management has said it wants to be the leading building-materials company in Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, and it is pushing exports into Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Australia and New Zealand while staying open to acquisitions at home and abroad [S9, S6]. FY2025 cash capex was 107.3 after a heavier 282.9 in FY2024, and it ran below depreciation because the big build was already done [S7]. The export push is the growth option that justifies a higher multiple than a domestic distributor; it is also the part of the plan with the least disclosure, so we treat it as bull-case upside rather than base case.

Ownership is concentrated and family-controlled, and it has not changed. At 31 December 2025 PT Tunggal Jaya Investama held 37.8% per cent, PT Harimas Tunggal Perkasa 35.6% per cent, both associated with the Tjiptodihardjo family, the founder a small direct stake, and the public 25.4% per cent [S9]. The note to the 30 September 2026 accounts shows the same blocks on the same issued capital, so no family block was sold [S8]. The IDX registry shows insiders at 79.2% and free float at 20.9%, above the exchange minimum [S0]; those figures use the exchange's narrower free-float definition, which excludes affiliated holders, and the company's own purchase of 222 m sharesm treasury shares in 2026 took those shares out of the float as well [S8]. There is no sell-down to reconcile: the draft's claim that the controlling shareholders sold through 2025 and 2026 is withdrawn.

On market position the honest answer is that the company publishes no market-share number and no industry body we could source publishes a reliable one for plastic roofing sheet. What the filings support is a premium branded position in a fragmented market, a distribution footprint that reaches beyond Java, and a range broad enough to fill a builder's merchant order [S9]. That is a challenger-to-leader position in a niche, not a dominant share of Indonesian building materials, and we report the evidence as thin rather than infer a share.

Indonesian building-materials demand is a derivative of household formation, renovation spending and middle-class consumption, tilted heavily to Java, which the annual report notes contributes the majority of national output and where household consumption is the main growth driver [S9]. The company's industry review points to manufacturing production and capital-goods imports rising in 2025, with the statistics agency recording import growth led by raw materials and capital goods, and to a recovery in construction after a soft patch [S9]. The same review is candid about the constraint: purchasing power among the middle class fell, regulation tightened, and global pressure weighed on supply chains and production costs [S9]. Demand for premium roofing is therefore growing, but it is discretionary renovation demand, not a protected infrastructure programme.

Plastic and composite roofing sits between commodity construction materials and consumer durables. It is sold through builders' merchants and specialist distributors, specified by contractors and chosen by homeowners on appearance, warranty and price. Manufacturing economics are a spread over resin, which is dollar-priced and imported; distribution economics are a spread over logistics and shelf space. Because sheet is bulky and cheap per kilogram, freight and local availability matter more than global scale, which is why regional plants and dense distribution are the durable advantages and why pure exporters struggle. Brand matters most in the premium tier, where warranty and colour range justify a price gap over unbranded sheet.

The input side is the swing factor. PVC resin, aluminium and specialty chemicals are dollar-priced imports, so the rupiah is a direct cost driver. The house macro deck has the rupiah at Rp18,228/USD to the dollar, weakening to Rp18,350/USD by FY2027E, with the policy rate at 5.8 rate per cent [S0]. A weaker rupiah raises the cost of every kilogram of resin and squeezes the gross margin unless the company passes it through; in 2025 it did, because the gross margin rose even as the currency weakened [S7]. Higher domestic rates are the second channel: they raise mortgage and developer funding costs, and the macro desk's tilt against Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic demand is a headwind for the property and renovation cycle that buys this company's products [S0].

Regulation is a modest moat rather than a threat. Indonesian building products need national standards certification, and the annual report flags tighter regulation as a sector risk [S9]. Compliance favours established manufacturers with testing and certification already in place, and local-content rules on public projects favour domestic plants. The offset is that imports from lower-cost Asian producers keep price competition intense in the commodity end, which is precisely why Impack positions in the premium tier.

Competition is fragmented. The group competes with Indonesian plastic-sheet makers, imported sheet from China and Vietnam, and substitutes such as metal roofing, fibre cement and clay tile [S9]. Switching costs are low for commodity sheet and higher in branded systems where the installer has been trained on the profile and fixing. The company's own account of its advantage is distribution and product breadth, not a patent or a network effect [S9]. That is a real but narrow moat: it protects the premium tier and the trade relationship and does not protect the group from a price war in standard sheet.

Five forces, briefly. Rivalry is high and rising with imports. Buyer power is moderate: distributors are fragmented, but large merchants can play suppliers against each other. Supplier power is high on resin, a globally priced commodity with few regional sellers, and low elsewhere. New entrants are a moderate threat: extrusion lines are not exotic, but a national brand, certification and a distribution network take years and capital. Substitutes pressure the commodity end steadily from metal and fibre cement, offset by plastic's weight, installation and corrosion advantages. The net is a business earning a good return in the premium tier and a poor one in commodity sheet, which is the mix the segment accounts show [S7].

On market share the evidence is qualitative. The company describes a qualified available market spanning Indonesia and export destinations and a distribution network built over decades, but it does not quantify share [S9]. We treat it as a leading premium brand in a fragmented niche, not a price-setting leader in Indonesian building materials, and we do not capitalise a share-gain story beyond the growth already in our revenue path.

FY2025 was a good year on a modest base. Revenue rose to 4,271.5 from 3,877.9 in FY2024, a 10.1% increase, with gross profit of 1,688.9 and a gross margin of 39.5% [S7]. Operating expenses of 840.4 left operating profit of 848.5, a 19.9% operating margin, and net profit attributable to shareholders of 620.0, or 11.3 per share [S7, S4]. The five-year record is steady margin expansion: revenue rose from 2,808.7 in FY2022 while the gross margin climbed from 34.8% and the operating margin from 15.9% [S4]. That is the profile of a company with pricing power in its niche and operating leverage in its factories.

Nine months of 2026 are stronger still, and the momentum is decelerating to a solid rate rather than fading. First-half revenue was IDR2,470.0bn and the second quarter alone grew by a third; the third quarter grew 12.0% per cent and net profit of IDR194.0bn rose by about a seventh [S10, S5]. Nine-month revenue reached 3,723 IDR bn and gross profit 1,488 IDR bn, a gross margin above the FY2025 rate, while profit before tax of 814 IDR bn and net profit attributable to shareholders of 640 IDR bn already exceed the whole of FY2025 [S8]. Finance costs fell year on year as short-term bank loans were repaid, a genuine improvement in the capital structure [S8]. The company kept its IDR5,100.0bn revenue target unchanged after the first half and again in October, and raised the net profit target to above IDR800.0bn in July [S10, S5]. Nine-month revenue is already about three-quarters of the plan and the implied fourth quarter is about a tenth higher year on year, in line with the third quarter's 12.0% per cent, so the plan is the current run-rate rather than a lag; the profit target leaves only a small fourth-quarter step [S10, S5].

The data pack needs one correction before any model is built on it. Indonesian issuers file cash-flow statements on the direct method, so the vendor's depreciation line is a fraction of the true charge; the LK's own reconciliation gives 184 IDR bn, of which 62.5 IDR bn is right-of-use depreciation on leases [S7]. The engine rebuilds D&A from those notes, so FY2025 EBITDA is 1,032.1 and the FY2025 charge is 183.6 [S7, S4]. Anyone reading the vendor data without that restatement overstates EBITDA by roughly a fifth.

Working capital is the defining feature of the cash flow, and the draft got its arithmetic wrong. Trade working capital at 31 December 2025 was IDR1,683.6bn — trade receivables including the related-party balance, plus inventories, less trade payables — about two-fifths of that year's revenue [S7]. The vendor reports a smaller measure because it nets prepayments and other current items against payables; using that as the opening base while modelling a trade ratio forward manufactured a one-off outflow in the forecast year that the business never incurred. We restate both historical years to the LK trade measure, IDR1,553.7bn at end-2024 against IDR1,683.6bn at end-2025, and hold 36.0% of revenue from FY2026E, close to the 30 September 2026 ratio, so the FY2026E increment is 152.5 rather than the larger figure the draft printed [S7, S8]. The ratio is high but falling, and it remains the main reason the DCF value sits far below the market price: growth consumes cash, and a wide distribution range needs inventory.

Capex is lumpy and currently light. Cash spending on property, plant and equipment was 107.3 in FY2025 after 282.9 in FY2024, when Batang, the Cikarang distribution centre and an acquisition were absorbing capital [S7, S9]. Nine-month 2026 cash capex and fixed-asset advances already exceed the whole of FY2025, so the underspend is over [S8]. Management had planned a larger programme for 2025 than it spent, and we model capex of 255.0 in FY2026E, easing toward four per cent of revenue by FY2030E, which is mid-cycle rather than a starvation assumption [S6]. D&A is modelled at 4.1% of revenue, consistent with the restated historical charge.

The balance sheet moved in 2026, and not because of the trading business. At 30 September 2026 cash was IDR562.0bn against net bank and lease debt of IDR535.3bn, compared with net debt of 325.2 at 31 December 2025 [S8, S0]. Net debt rose because of capital returns and leases, not an operating burn: nine-month operating cash flow was positive and covered investing outflows, while the company spent IDR451.7bn buying its own shares and paid down lease liabilities [S8]. The interim dividend the company declared for 2026 went ex on 22 October, after the balance-sheet date, and is bridged in the valuation. The company is therefore not moving to net cash this year, and the draft's net-cash narrative is withdrawn; our forecast balance-sheet line for FY2026E of -63.2 rolls from 31 December 2025 and does not carry the treasury purchase as an outflow, so it reads as the trading cash generated in the year, not as the actual position, which the 30 September balance sheet states. The debt is bank facilities and leases rather than public bonds [S7, S8].

Equity tells the same story. It rose to 3,398.0 at end-2025 from 2,144.9, but not through a revaluation: the increase came from retained profit plus 586 IDR bn of proceeds from a non-preemptive rights issue, which is real cash and not an accounting uplift [S7, S9]. That matters because the method card warns about revaluation-inflated book value in Indonesian industrials; this one is clean, which is why we are willing to use book as a cross-check. In 2026 the equity account absorbed a 452 IDR bn treasury-share debit on top of profit [S8].

Capital allocation has been growth-first and, in 2026, expensive for continuing holders. The company paid no cash dividend for FY2024, retaining the entire 539 IDR bn of that year's profit for working capital and expansion, then raised 586 IDR bn of new equity in 2025 at a price well below today's [S6, S7, S8]. In 2026 it bought 222 m sharesm shares back for 452 IDR bn, an average of more than twice today's price [S8]. At our estimate of value that transfer went to the shareholders who sold, and it is the clearest sign that management's view of intrinsic value is far above ours. The company has since declared an interim dividend for 2026, and we model a payout of 35.0%, close to the interim distribution relative to our FY2026E profit [S0]. Shareholders have funded growth twice, by forgoing dividends and by buying new shares, and have had cash returned once, at a price that destroyed value.

Earnings quality screens are mostly reassuring but not clean. Accruals are negative: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025, and free cash flow to the firm of 606.4 covered the working-capital build and capex [S7]. Receivables grew more slowly than revenue in the first nine months, which is a good sign [S8]. Inventory is the flag we carry: it rose faster than cost of sales in FY2025, driven by finished goods, and the impairment allowance reached IDR53.1bn after a charge more than five times the prior year's [S7]. By 30 September 2026 inventory stood at IDR1,446.6bn [S8]. That is consistent with a wider product range and new subsidiaries, which is the company's explanation, but the note gives no ageing table, so we cannot verify it; we carry it as an open flag and put a write-down in the bear case rather than assume it away. There is no capitalised development programme to speak of and the audit opinion is unmodified [S9].

Related-party flows are small in the trading business and large in capital transactions. FY2025 sales to related parties were IDR0.2bn, a rounding error against revenue, and related-party receivables are similarly immaterial [S7]. The capital account is different: equity carries a IDR677.0bn debit for transactions with under-common-control entities, almost all of it the premium paid for Mulford Holdings, an Australian acquisition priced far above the book value of the net assets received [S7]. That is a completed transfer of value to a related party, about a fifth of FY2025 equity, not an optics item. It does not affect forward cash flow, but it tells you the price at which this family does deals with itself, and the company has said it remains open to further acquisitions at home and abroad [S9, S7].

Our forecast takes FY2026E revenue to 5,100.1, the company's own plan, with a 40.0% gross margin held at the nine-month actual and an operating margin of 23.0% [S10, S8]. That operating margin is above the reported FY2025 figure for two sourced reasons: SG&A fell to 17.0% of revenue net of recurring other income, which ran at IDR54.6bn in the first nine months and a similar share a year earlier and is received in cash inside operating activities, and gross margin rose [S8]. We then fade growth from 14.0% in FY2027E to 10.0% in FY2030E and to terminal growth after that, holding the gross margin flat at 40.0% and the net SG&A ratio flat rather than assuming the observed operating leverage reverses [S7]. Earnings per share reach 25.1 by FY2030E and return on equity stays near 20.4% [S0]. The growth is manufactured the honest way: a reinvestment rate of roughly half of NOPAT at incremental returns in the high teens, which supports high-single to low-double-digit growth, not the rate the price implies.

We value Impack primarily on a discounted free cash flow to the firm model, with earnings and EBITDA multiples as cross-checks. The choice fits the industry: building materials is capital-intensive, cyclical growth where value depends on volume, margin and the working capital needed to support both, and a single-year multiple captures neither the growth run nor the capital intensity. The house compounder card asks for the reinvestment rate, the incremental return, a pinned discount rate, a fade and a multiple-survival test; we take each in turn.

The cost of capital is pinned inside the house band. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the Indonesia country premium 2.5% and the industry unlevered beta 0.80, which levers to 0.82 at the company's modest net debt [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 11.3% and, with debt at 9.4% pre-tax and a 22.0% tax rate, a WACC of 11.2%, inside the IDR band the method card sets [S0].

The DCF produces Rp276 per share. Free cash flow to the firm is 714.2 in FY2026E, held back by the working-capital build, then 760.1 as growth moderates and the working-capital ratio falls, rising through the forecast as capex intensity falls [S7]. Terminal value, growing at 4.0% and discounted at the WACC, is 57.3% of enterprise value, high but not unusual for a growth franchise; it is also the part most exposed to the growth assumption, which is why we test it below [S0].

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative. The peer-median P/E of 7.6 times applied to FY2025 net profit gives Rp86, -68.9% below the DCF; the peer-median EV/EBITDA multiple of 5.3 times gives Rp80 [S0]. The peer set is dominated by Indonesian cement, ceramics, cable and sanitary ware that earn lower returns on capital and grow more slowly than Impack, so a peer-median multiple is a floor for a premium franchise, not a fair value, and the gap to the DCF is what a floor looks like. That is why the DCF now carries 85.0% of the target and the two multiples keep 10.0% and 5.0% only as a discipline on terminal-value optimism: at 7.6 times earnings even a good industrial would be priced for stagnation. The revised target of Rp277 is therefore close to the DCF, and the rating does not depend on the multiple blend: on the DCF alone the shares are worth Rp276, still far below the Rp775 price [S0].

The multiple-survival test is the heart of the call. At our target the shares would trade on Rp277 against FY2026E earnings of 15.6, a multiple consistent with a mid-teens grower earning a high-teens return on equity; at the market price the multiple is 49.8x, and on FY2027E earnings it is still 43.2x [S0]. Even our own DCF assumes the multiple compresses hard: the terminal value capitalises FY2035 EBITDA at a single-digit multiple, against the 30.8x entry multiple today [S0]. A buyer at today's price is paying an entry multiple that a later buyer could only justify with acceleration from here. That is multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume, and it is the base-rate trap the method card flags for Indonesian premium names.

What the price implies is the cleanest way to say it. Running the DCF backwards, today's Rp775 requires revenue growth of 32.9% in FY2027E, and because the solver applies that increment to every forecast year the requirement is a sustained path of high-twenties growth through FY2030E and mid-twenties growth to FY2035E, not a one-year jump. For comparison our base grows 14.0% in FY2027E and the company plans IDR5,100.0bn of FY2026 revenue that it has kept unchanged [S10]. The alternative route to the same price is a discount rate below the 7.4% ten-year sovereign yield, which no Indonesian mid-cap should command. That is not a small optimism gap; it is a different company and a different country risk premium.

The valuation is most sensitive to the gross margin, the working-capital ratio and the length of the growth run. A two-point gross margin miss, which is what a sustained weak rupiah and an inability to pass resin costs through would produce, removes roughly a fifth of the DCF value; holding working capital a few points higher for the forecast cuts it by a similar order; and shortening the high-growth phase by three years removes more than a quarter. The sensitivity table sets these out. We have not padded any of them: the base case carries the company's own unchanged FY2026 plan, the actual nine-month margin and the actual 30 September trade working capital [S10, S8, S7].

The main downside is the price itself. A -63.5% expected return is the arithmetic of a good business valued at a growth rate it has not sustained; the risk to our call is that growth does accelerate and the multiple proves justified, which is the bull case below. Beyond the multiple, the operating risks are real and mostly external.

**Property and renovation demand.** Premium roofing is discretionary. A weaker property cycle, higher mortgage rates or a further squeeze on middle-class purchasing power would slow volume; the company names exactly this as its main demand constraint [S9]. Likelihood high over a twelve-month horizon given the macro desk's tilt against Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic demand. Impact high, because operating leverage amplifies a volume miss [S0].

**Currency and resin cost.** Resin is dollar-priced and imported, and the house deck has the rupiah weakening further [S0]. A cost spike that cannot be passed through compresses the gross margin, the single most valuable variable in the model. Likelihood medium, impact high.

**Competition and imports.** Lower-cost Asian sheet and substitutes cap pricing in the standard tier; a price war would hurt volume and margin [S9]. Likelihood medium, impact medium, because the premium tier is stickier.

**Inventory.** Inventory is above a year of cost of sales and grew ahead of cost of sales in FY2025, with the allowance at IDR53.1bn [S7, S8]. A demand stall would force markdowns beyond that allowance. Likelihood medium, impact low to medium: a write-down of a tenth of the IDR1,446.6bn on the 30 September balance sheet would cost about a point and a half of DCF value.

**Governance and capital allocation.** The controlling family owns the great majority of the shares and has used the balance sheet to buy back stock at more than twice our estimate of value and to acquire a related-party business at a large premium to book [S8, S7]. Neither is a manipulation-class flag; both are value-transfer risks that argue for a governance discount rather than a premium. Likelihood of further such transactions medium, impact medium through both cash and the multiple.

**Execution on expansion.** Batang, the uPVC lines and the Australian FRP expansion are the growth engine; delays or a demand shortfall would leave depreciation without revenue [S9]. Likelihood medium, impact medium.

**Liquidity.** The shares trade a healthy daily value and the free float clears the exchange minimum, so a position can be exited; the risk is price impact in a de-rating, not an inability to trade [S0]. Likelihood low, impact low.

The bear case assumes growth four points lower and the gross margin two points lower than base, the mirror of the bull case. It produces Rp195, because the working-capital and capex burden does not fall with revenue and the multiple compresses on lower growth [S0]. The bull case assumes growth four points higher and the gross margin two points higher, capturing a faster export ramp and a stronger rupiah, and produces Rp375 [S0]. The probability-weighted target is Rp277. The asymmetry is honest: even the bull case is far below the current price, which is the point of the call.

**What would justify today's price.** Two paths exist and neither is a fundamental value, so neither is in the scenario table. The first is the reverse-DCF path above: 32.9% revenue growth in FY2027E sustained for a decade at high-twenties growth with the gross margin held, which would make Impack several times its current size. The second is a cost of capital below the Indonesian sovereign yield. An investor who believes either should own the stock; we cannot source evidence for either, and the company's own unchanged plan and its third-quarter revenue growth point the other way [S10, S5].

**Take-private and tender risk.** This is the most credible way we are wrong, and it is why the conviction behind a SELL is bounded. Insiders hold 79.2% per cent of the company and the free float is 20.9% per cent, exactly the structure in which a controlling family can make a tender offer at a price that clears the market and still looks cheap to it [S0]. The family bought 222 m sharesm shares in 2026 at an average of more than twice today's price, and its own acquisition accounting implies it values related assets well above book [S8, S7]. A tender at or above Rp775 would defeat a SELL even though it is several times our estimate of value, and a minority holder has no veto. We do not put it in the probability-weighted target because it is a price event rather than a cash-flow outcome, but it belongs in the risk list. Any disclosure of a tender, a delisting plan or a further large buyback would be a signal to re-underwrite rather than to add.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A FY2026 gross margin above the nine-month rate in a weaker rupiah would show genuine pricing power; export revenue disclosed by destination, at scale, would validate the regional strategy. On the other side, a working-capital ratio that keeps rising, inventory write-downs beyond the current allowance, capex running ahead of depreciation without revenue, or a further buyback at a premium to intrinsic value would confirm the capital-intensity and capital-allocation problems. We would revisit the rating if the shares fell to where the DCF value and the price met, which is a long way from here.

Ownership is concentrated in the founding family and stable. Tunggal Jaya Investama held 37.8% per cent, Harimas Tunggal Perkasa 35.6% per cent and the founder a small direct stake at the end of 2025, with the public at 25.4% per cent [S9]. The same blocks appear unchanged in the 30 September 2026 accounts, so there was no family sell-down in 2026; the IDX registry's 20.9% per cent free float and 79.2% per cent insider figure are a narrower definition that excludes affiliated holders and the 222 m sharesm treasury shares [S0, S8]. The stock is not on the special monitoring board [S0]. The draft's sell-down claim, and the supply-overhang risk built on it, are withdrawn.

The 2025 non-preemptive rights issue raised 586 IDR bn and enlarged the share count modestly [S7]. It was a sensible way to fund expansion without adding debt, but it diluted existing holders and it came in a year when no dividend was paid for FY2024 [S6]. The company has since resumed distributions with an interim dividend for 2026, and we expect a payout of 35.0% [S0]. The dividend record is improving but young, and shareholders should not treat the current distribution as a policy commitment.

Three structural items deserve attention. The annual meeting approved pledging group assets worth more than half of net assets as collateral for financing, common practice in Indonesia but it reduces the unencumbered asset base and constrains future flexibility [S6]. The balance sheet carries a IDR677.0bn common-control transaction difference that reduces equity, almost all of it the premium paid for Mulford Holdings; we classify it as a completed value transfer to a related party, about a fifth of FY2025 equity, not an optics item [S7]. And the 2026 treasury purchase spent 452 IDR bn on 222 m sharesm shares, 452 IDR bn of cash for a small slice of the company, at an average price more than twice today's [S8]. Related-party trading flows are immaterial: sales to related parties were 0.2 IDR bn in FY2025, effectively nothing against revenue [S7]. None of these is a manipulation-class flag; the capital transactions are value-transfer and capital-allocation flags, and they argue for a governance discount rather than a premium.

The audit is clean and the auditor changed in FY2025, from Gani Sigiro & Handayani to Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan, both unmodified opinions [S9]. A change of auditor is worth noting but not alarming in this direction: the new firm is the larger one. An independent commissioner joined in 2025 and the governance structure follows the Indonesian code [S6, S9]. Related-party sales and receivables are immaterial relative to revenue, but the group structure with a property subsidiary and several manufacturing entities leaves room for transfer pricing that the disclosures do not fully illuminate, and the common-control history shows the family is willing to transact at prices well above book [S7].

On ESG the main exposure is plastic. Impack is a plastics converter, so resin sourcing, recyclability and waste are the material issues; its response has been the recycled-roofing line that processes multilayer plastic waste into building sheet, a genuine product rather than a reporting exercise [S9]. Energy use in extrusion is the second exposure, and the company reports efficiency and certification programmes in the annual report [S9]. Social and governance metrics are standard for an Indonesian mid-cap: a small workforce relative to revenue because distribution runs through merchants, and a concentrated ownership structure that limits minority influence [S9, S0].

The dated catalysts are the audited FY2026 results in the first quarter of 2027, which will show whether the nine-month margin held in the fourth quarter and whether the working-capital build unwound; the annual meeting and dividend resolution in mid-2027; and the quarterly reports after that, each a demand read after the uPVC and Batang line additions [S8, S9]. On the cost side, year-end resin contracts and the rupiah fix are the markers for the FY2027 gross margin, and the policy rate path is the marker for property demand [S0].

The KPIs we watch are revenue growth against the unchanged company plan and against the third quarter's 12.0% per cent, the gross margin against the nine-month rate, inventory and receivable days against revenue growth, cash capex against depreciation, net debt against the 535 IDR bn reported at 30 September, any further treasury purchases or related-party transactions, and disclosure of export revenue by destination [S7, S8, S0]. We also watch for any tender or delisting disclosure, the one event that would invalidate a SELL at this price.

Between updates the monitoring rule is simple. If the price falls to the DCF value and the operating evidence holds, the rating changes; until then, a good company at a demanding price remains a sell [S0, S7]. We would rather be early and wrong on timing than late and wrong on value.

bear.narrative: Property and middle-class demand stall, imported PVC resin stays expensive on a weak rupiah, and the multiple stays compressed after the buyback: revenue growth is 4pp lower and gross margin 2pp lower than base, mirrored against the bull case.

bull.narrative: Construction and renovation demand re-accelerates, the Australia/New Zealand FRP and uPVC export lines scale faster than planned, and premium mix adds 2pp of gross margin with 4pp more revenue growth, mirroring the bear case.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company plan: Rp 5.10trn revenue guidance, kept unchanged in July 2026 after H1 revenue of Rp 2.47trn (+29.7%) and again in October (S10); 9M2026 revenue of Rp 3.72trn (S8) leaves Rp 1.38trn for Q4, +10.4% yoy against Q3 2026 growth of 12% (S5) and Q4 2025 revenue of Rp 1.25trn, so the plan is the current run-rate, not a lag. FY2027-30 taper to 10% as Indonesian building-material demand grows high single digit and the ASEAN/Australia/New Zealand export push (S6) builds from a small base; long-run 6% is nominal GDP, not a market-share fantasy.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin was 39.97% (gross profit Rp 1,488.3bn on revenue Rp 3,723.3bn, S8) and FY2025 was 39.54% (S7); premium Alderon/Solartuff mix and factory efficiency offset imported PVC resin and a weak rupiah. Held at the last actual 40.0% through FY2030E and in perpetuity; no margin fade is assumed because the FY2022-9M2026 record is 34.8% to 39.97% and rising, and the fourth quarter of 2026 carries the only sourced risk (management flags resin, rupiah, freight and rates, S5).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue, net of recurring other income
assumptions.basis: Reported operating expenses were 18.34% of 9M2026 revenue and 19.68% of FY2025 revenue (S7/S8), while other income - net was Rp54.6bn in 9M2026 and Rp42.3bn in 9M2025 (1.47% and 1.46% of revenue, S8 F50) and is received in cash inside operating activities. We therefore model SG&A net of that recurring stream: 18.34% less 1.47% = 16.87% at the last actual, rounded to 17.0% and held flat. Modelling other income below EBIT would drop a recurring ~1.3% of revenue out of the FCFF the DCF capitalises.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total FY2025 D&A was Rp 183.6bn (EBITDA Rp 1,032.1bn less operating profit Rp 848.5bn, S4), i.e. 4.30% of revenue; the LK notes split it into PPE depreciation Rp 106.3bn, right-of-use depreciation Rp 62.5bn and intangible amortisation (S7). Lease renewals for warehouses and the Batang plant keep the charge near 4%.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash capex was Rp 107.3bn in FY2025 (2.5% of revenue) after Rp 242.3bn in FY2024 (6.2%) as the Batang and Cikarang lines completed; the 2025 plan was Rp 345bn (S6), and the company keeps adding uPVC/FRP lines (S9). We model 5.0% in FY2026E falling to 4.2%, i.e. mid-cycle between the 2024 build and the 2025 underspend.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Trade operating working capital from the LK is Rp1,683.6bn at 31 Dec 2025 (trade receivables 787.3 including Rp56.7bn related-party + inventories 1,279.0 - trade payables 382.8, F44) = 39.4% of revenue; at 30 Sep 2026 it is Rp1,807.2bn (receivables 786.3 + inventories 1,446.6 - payables 425.7) = 36.4% of LTM revenue. We hold 36% from FY2026E, the current balance-sheet ratio, rather than the 31.9% in the data pack (which nets prepayments and other current items) or the FY2025 39.4% peak.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax expense Rp 178.3bn on pre-tax profit Rp 801.8bn = 22.2% (S7); 9M2026 was 20.2% (S8). Statutory 22% with final tax on property income, so 22.2% flat.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 financial costs were Rp 98.7bn (S7) on average borrowings of about Rp 1.4trn = 7.0%; 9M2026 financial costs fell to Rp 52.8bn (S8) as short-term bank loans were repaid, so 7.0% is the top of the observed range.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income Rp 9.06bn (S7) on opening cash of Rp 724bn = 1.25%; 9M2026 finance income Rp 8.5bn (S8) is consistent.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: 9M2026 shows net bank borrowing roughly flat (short-term loans drawn Rp1,583bn against Rp1,426bn repaid, long-term receipts Rp63bn against Rp195bn repaid, S8) and no new long-term facility; the one-off Rp451.7bn treasury-share purchase (F47) is a cash outflow already inside the 30 Sep 2026 net debt used in the valuation bridge, so it is not modelled again as borrowing.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero here because the recurring stream is already carried inside opex_pct, net of SG&A: other income - net was Rp66.9bn less Rp21.6bn expenses in FY2025 (S7) and Rp54.6bn in 9M2026 (F50), i.e. 1.3-1.5% of revenue in consecutive periods. Adding it again below EBIT would double count.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 non-controlling interest was Rp 9.1bn of Rp 649.3bn net profit = 1.4% (S8); FY2025 was 0.6% (S7). The 50.95%-owned property subsidiary is the swing factor, so 1.0% is used.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The October 2026 interim dividend of Rp 273.42bn (Rp 5 per share) is 34% of our FY2026E net profit; FY2023 paid 42.5% and FY2024 paid nothing (S6). 35% reflects a growing but still reinvestment-heavy company.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No further issuance assumed after the FY2025 non-preemptive rights issue took the share count to 54,907m (S7); the placement is complete.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4% is below long-run Indonesian nominal GDP growth of roughly 6-7% and below the 6% revenue growth we fade to, appropriate for a building-materials franchise whose terminal growth cannot exceed the economy.

challenges.challenge: Target Rp198 is 32% below the report's own Rp240 DCF because 40% of the blend is 7.59x P/E and 5.26x EV/EBITDA from ARNA, TOTO, SPTO, SCCO and MARK, which the report itself calls a floor for a premium franchise, not fair value. A knowingly inappropriate multiple is being used as two-fifths of fair value.
challenges.answer: Re-weighted to 0.85 DCF / 0.10 P/E / 0.05 EV/EBITDA and stated the peer set is a floor, not fair value. Target rises to 277 against a DCF of 276, so the SELL survives on the DCF alone at about -64% from the 775 price [S0].

challenges.challenge: The base case uses the April plan of Rp5,100bn revenue, which implies Q4-2026 revenue of about 1,377 (+10.3% yoy) after 9M revenue of 3,723 (+23.1%) and 9M net profit of 640 already above all of FY2025. The analyst's own post-BS note says the 2026 target was raised after 9M but neither sources nor uses it; Q4 is seasonally the strongest quarter (29% of FY2025 revenue).
challenges.answer: The revenue guidance was not raised: the company kept Rp5.10trn for FY2026 after H1 and again in October, and only the net profit target moved up to above Rp800bn. 9M revenue of Rp3.72trn leaves about a tenth growth for Q4, in line with Q3's 12%, so the plan is the run-rate [S10, S5, S8].

challenges.challenge: Sections 1, 5 and 6 assert the controlling shareholders reduced holdings through 2025 and 2026 and that this raised the free float, cited to S9, an FY2025 annual report that cannot cover 2026. The report's own S0 figures point the other way: public 25.45% at end-2025 (F41) versus free float 20.9% and insiders 79.2% now.
challenges.answer: The sell-down claim is withdrawn: the 30 Sep 2026 accounts show Tunggal Jaya at 37.81% and the public at 25.45% on the same capital, so no block was sold. The lower free float is the exchange's narrower definition plus the 221.7m treasury shares bought in 2026 [S8, S9, S0].

challenges.challenge: The bull case is Rp257, 33% of the Rp775 price, so no modelled state of the world puts the stock within 60% of the market. There is also no acquisition or take-private path although insiders hold 79.2% of a company with a 20.9% float, which is a standard squeeze risk against a SELL with 74% downside.
challenges.answer: Added an explicit upside section naming the reverse-DCF path (32.9% growth sustained) and a discount rate below the sovereign yield, plus a take-private paragraph: insiders 79.2% and a 20.9% float, with the family buying at more than twice today's price. The mirrored bull now values the shares at 374.5, still far below 775 [S8, S0].

challenges.challenge: The Rp677.0bn debit in equity for transactions with under-common-control entities (S7 note 25) is 20% of FY2025 equity and about Rp12.4 per share, a completed transfer to related parties, not an optics item. The report also never quantifies related-party flow as a share of revenue, which the house earnings-quality card requires.
challenges.answer: Classified the Rp677.0bn common-control debit as a completed value transfer, about a fifth of FY2025 equity, mostly the Mulford Holdings premium, and quantified related-party sales at Rp0.245bn, effectively nil against revenue [S7].

challenges.challenge: Inventory rose 14.4% to Rp1,279bn in FY2025 while COGS rose 9.8%, a divergence flag under the house earnings-quality card, and inventory is 30% of revenue. The report dismisses it as new subsidiaries and product lines without citing the inventory note or the ageing.
challenges.answer: Cited the inventory note: allowance Rp53.1bn after a charge more than five times the prior year, finished goods leading the build, no ageing table. Carried as an open flag with a write-down sensitivity in the risks section [S7, S8].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says the FY2026E revenue increase alone absorbs Rp422.1bn of working capital. At 35% the increment is Rp290.0bn; the other Rp132.1bn is a one-off step-up from the pack's Rp1,362.9bn (31.9%) base, while the LK components (receivables 787.3 plus inventory 1,279.0 less payables 382.8) give Rp1,683.5bn, 39.4% of revenue. The DCF's first forecast year therefore carries a cash outflow the business did not incur.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt trade working capital from the LK: Rp1,683.6bn at Dec-2025 (39.4%) and Rp1,807.2bn at 30 Sep 2026 (36.4%), modelled at 36%. The FY2026E increment is Rp152.5bn, not Rp422.1bn, and the sentence is corrected [S7, S8].

challenges.challenge: The model shows FY2026E net debt of Rp258.0bn, but the bridge correctly uses Rp529.8bn at 30 September 2026 and the company paid a Rp273.4bn dividend on 22 October. Net debt rose about Rp205bn in the first nine months of 2026, so the claim that the company moves to net cash is contradicted by the actual balance-sheet trend, and section 3 still quotes the stale 31 December 2025 figure of Rp325.2bn as if current.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now runs from the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet: cash Rp562.0bn, net bank and lease debt Rp535.3bn, up from Rp325.2bn at Dec-2025 because of the Rp451.7bn buyback and leases. The net-cash narrative is withdrawn and the forecast line's limitation is disclosed [S8, S0].

challenges.challenge: Gross margin is faded from 40.0% to 39.0% and opex raised from 18.3% to 19.0% by FY2031 with no source, against a four-year record of gross margin 34.8 to 39.5 to 39.97% (9M2026) and EBIT margin 15.9 to 19.9 to 21.6%. The base case assumes the observed operating leverage reverses.
challenges.answer: Gross margin held at the 9M2026 39.97% (40.0%) through FY2030E and in perpetuity, and SG&A held flat at 17.0% of revenue net of other income, so the observed operating leverage is no longer reversed [S8, S7].

challenges.challenge: Other non-operating income is held at zero although FY2025 had net other income of about Rp45.3bn and 9M2026 shows about Rp52bn (PBT 813.5 versus EBIT 805.6 less net finance cost 44.3), i.e. it appears in two consecutive periods and looks recurring.
challenges.answer: Recurring other income is now inside EBIT: reported SG&A of 18.34% of 9M2026 revenue less other income of 1.47% gives 16.87%, modelled at 17.0%, and other_nonop is zero to avoid double counting [S8, S7].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is reported as requiring 37.9% revenue growth in FY2027E, but the engine's factor of +23.9pp is applied from FY2027 onward, so the requirement is about 38% sustained and only slowly fading, not a one-year jump; the same misdescription underpins the extreme_call justification. The multiple-survival test also gives no number: terminal value implies about 8.2x EBITDA versus 32.6x entry.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF is now described as a sustained path: 32.9% growth in FY2027E, high twenties to FY2030E and mid twenties to FY2035E, or a discount rate below the 7.45% sovereign yield. The multiple-survival test now states that terminal value capitalises FY2035 EBITDA in single digits against 30.8x entry [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: No scenario values the stock above Rp257, 33% of the Rp775 price; the 79.2% insider stake makes a take-private or squeeze risk the SELL never considers, and the five-country export platform is assigned to the bull case only.

missing_bear_case.note: The Rp677bn common-control debit (20% of equity, S7 note 25) is labelled optics-class though it is a completed related-party transfer, and inventory +14.4% vs COGS +9.8% is asserted benign without citing the inventory note.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue 5,100 implies Q4-2026 growth of 10.3% after 9M +23.1% and rests on April guidance the analyst's own post-BS review says was raised after 9M; gross margin fades 40.0 to 39.0% and opex rises 18.3 to 19.0% against a four-year improving trend.

evidence_and_citations.note: Guidance (S3), 9M P&L (S8), D&A 183.6, capex 107.3, the asset-pledge resolution (S6) and the Tanubrata auditor (S9) all verify. But the 2026 family sell-down that raised the free float is cited to the FY2025 annual report and contradicted by S0, which shows public 25.45% at end-2025 vs 20.9% now.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary is correct for capital-intensive building materials and WACC 11.19% sits in the 11-13% band, but 40% of the blend uses a 7.59x P/E and 5.26x EV/EBITDA median from cement, ceramics and metal peers the report itself calls a floor, not fair value; the implied exit multiple is never stated.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose outruns evidence: working capital is called the single most important reason the DCF sits below the price, yet 35% is below the LK-derived 39.4%; and a distribution whose bull case is -67% below price cannot express the market being right.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck values are used correctly (FX 18,350 FY2027E, BI 5.75) but the text prints 5.8 rate per cent and never links the FX/resin path to the gross-margin line although FX is called the swing factor; peer inputs for INDUSTRIAL_GOODS are read on the same basis.

conservatism_audit.note: Stacked below the last actual or the company's own data: NWC stepped 31.9 to 35.0% (a 132bn one-off), other income zeroed despite 45bn FY2025 and about 52bn 9M2026, gross margin 40.0 to 39.0%, opex 18.3 to 19.0%, terminal g 4% vs 5.3% real GDP. Worth roughly 8-10% of the DCF, not the rating.

calibration.note: FY2026E EBITDA margin 25.8% vs FY2025A 24.16% (+1.64pp) is sourced to 9M2026 gross margin 39.97% and opex 18.34%, so the drift is explained, and the extreme_call BLOCK is answered with three sourced drivers plus a reverse DCF.

signoff.notes: The SELL survives on the DCF alone at Rp276 after the fixes the review forced: gross margin held at the 9M2026 actual 40.0%, working capital rebuilt from the LK at 36% (not the 39.4% year-end), net debt from the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet, and the October interim dividend deducted as a post-balance-sheet item. Peer multiples now carry only 15% and are stated as a floor. The 49.8x FY2026E P/E against a kept 19.4% plan is the evidence, the reverse DCF path (32.9% sustained) and the take-private risk at Rp775 are both disclosed, and every scenario including the bull at Rp375 sits below the price. C1-C11 answered. Approve.

bias.note: Base case is the company plan (revenue 5,100.1 vs the Rp5,100bn guidance kept unchanged [S10]) at the 9M2026 gross margin 39.97% [S8] and SG&A net of other income 16.87% [S8]; no volume, grade or margin haircut, capex 5.0% vs 2.5% FY2025 and terminal g 4% below nominal GDP. The one unsupported optimism is carrying FX-driven other income (Rp62.8bn of the Rp54.6bn net, S8 note 35) inside EBITDA in perpetuity, about 7% of DCF; the risk text overstates two downside sensitivities (Q2, Q3). Net direction neutral: the SELL survives the bull case at 375 vs the 775 price.

findings.finding: FY2026E net debt (-63.2) and equity (3,977.4) roll from 31 Dec 2025 and omit the Rp451.7bn treasury purchase already in the 30 Sep 2026 accounts (F47, S8) and the Rp273.4bn interim dividend, so the summary 10.7x book is a forward-equity artefact; the DCF bridge correctly uses 529.8 net debt and 254.0 minorities.
The investment summary and section 4 say a two-point gross margin miss removes roughly a fifth of the DCF value; the engine sensitivity grid gives 242.1 vs 269.9, minus 10.3%.

Section 5 says inventory is above a year of cost of sales; inventory is Rp1,446.6bn at 30 Sep 2026 (F51) against annualised 9M COGS of about Rp2,980bn, about six months, and FY2025 is 1,279.0/2,582.6 = 0.50 years.
Section 6 states the AGM approved pledging group assets worth more than half of net assets [S6]; archived S6 (2,284 chars) contains no pledge text and S7/S8/S9 contain no matching disclosure.
The weights.changed justification says FY2025 ROE was 15%; FY2025 ROE is 22.4% (620.0 on average equity 2,771.5, S4/S7) and the report itself says 22.4%.

Opex 17.0% nets out recurring other income of 1.47% of revenue, but S8 note 35 shows the Rp54.6bn is mostly an FX gain (Rp62.8bn) with inventory, impairment and tax offsets, not a stable operating stream; holding it in EBITDA in perpetuity adds about 7% to the DCF and drives part of the 2.94pp calibration gap to FY2025A.

The bear case applies -4pp revenue growth every year, taking FY2031-35 growth to about 2% while terminal g stays 4%, so the bear terminal value assumes re-acceleration; the bear -28% / bull +39% value asymmetry is asserted as honest without a source.
Section 6 says the stock is not on the special monitoring board [S0] but omits that S9 records a 2025 trading suspension for a significant cumulative share-price rise.

flags.message: expected return -64%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The large negative return is the multiple, not a cautious base case. Price 775 is 49.8x our FY2026E EPS and 10.7x book [S0], and the reverse DCF solves to 32.9% revenue growth in FY2027E sustained at high-twenties through FY2030E and mid-twenties to FY2035E, against a company plan of Rp 5.10trn revenue for FY2026 (+19.4% on FY2025) that it has kept unchanged [S10] and Q3 2026 revenue growth of 12% [S5]. Every input is at or better than the last actual: gross margin held at the 9M2026 39.97% with no fade [S8], SG&A net of recurring other income at the 16.87% actual [S8], trade working capital at the 30 Sep 2026 36.4% of LTM revenue [S8], D&A at the LK restated 4.1% of revenue [S7], and capex at 5.0% falling to 4.2%, mid-cycle against FY2024 6.2% and FY2025 2.5% [S7]. Nothing is haircut for caution; the headroom sits in the bull case, which still values the shares far below the price [S0].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'pe': 0.25, 'ev_ebitda': 0.15}
flags.justification: DCF raised to 85% from 60% because the peer set (ARNA, MARK, SCCO, SPTO, TOTO) is Indonesian cement, ceramics, cable and sanitary ware, distributing 7.6x P/E and 5.3x EV/EBITDA [S0]; the report itself calls that a floor for a premium franchise earning a FY2025 ROE of 15% on a 39.5% gross margin [S7], and a floor cannot carry two-fifths of fair value. The 15% left to P/E and EV/EBITDA disciplines terminal-value optimism rather than stating value.
